definition: To come together, or bring people together, for a formal meeting.
example: The judges will convene at noon to choose the winning painting.
nuance: Convene suggests a planned, purposeful meeting, while congregate can describe any crowd that gathers, even casually.
prompt: A city council must respond quickly to a broken water main downtown.
options: The mayor asked the council to convene an emergency session that evening.
The engineer hoped to convene the residents that their tap water was still safe to drink.
Once the vote was over, the members began to convene and headed home in separate cars.
A lone clerk decided to convene by herself at her desk.
reasons: Calling officials together for an urgent, official session is the word's core use.
This confuses the word with convince; you persuade people of a claim, you don't assemble them of it.
Leaving and scattering after a meeting is adjourning, the reverse of coming together.
One person alone cannot hold a meeting; the word requires a group.

practice.prompt: A high school science club is planning its first meeting of the year.
options: She tried to convene the new club rules to everyone through a long email.
After the final vote, the members began to convene, drifting out of the lab one by one.
Two students happened to convene by chance at the water fountain between classes.
The president will convene the members in the lab on Friday.
reasons: Rules are passed along, not assembled; this mixes the word up with convey.
Drifting away describes a group breaking up, not gathering.
A random run-in lacks the planning and purpose that the word implies.
Summoning the group to a set place and time for an organized meeting fits exactly.
